Massachusetts Gaming Commission Investigates Alleged Proxy Betting on Bill Simmons's FanDuel Account

Published November 6, 2026 · 3 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Massachusetts Gaming Commission has opened a formal inquiry into alleged proxy betting tied to media personality Bill Simmons's FanDuel account, after the sportsbook itself flagged the activity to the regulator. Commissioners were briefed on the matter this week and voted to schedule an adjudicatory hearing, meaning the case is still pending rather than resolved.

What FanDuel reported

According to a memo cited by Covers.com, FanDuel identified 22 wagers totaling $21,800 in handle placed on Simmons's account on August 5, 7, and 19, 2026. The sportsbook voided the wagers and took action on the account after investigating. The matter came to light publicly after Simmons discussed on an August 30 podcast episode that someone else had placed bets on his behalf in Massachusetts — a practice commonly known as proxy betting, where a person physically located in a licensed state places wagers for someone who isn't there themselves.

Why regulators treat this seriously

Proxy betting runs against the core identity-and-location rules that underpin legal, regulated sports betting in every US state: a wager has to be placed by the account holder, physically within a state where that operator is licensed, full stop. Commissioner Eileen O'Brien said she was "a little disturbed" by any suggestion that the rule against proxy betting wasn't well understood, while Commission Chair Jordan Maynard said he was "more interested in how the operator let something like this happen" and in what FanDuel did once it found out. Senior enforcement counsel Zachary Mercer said the bureau "hasn't foreclosed any kind of condition" as the case moves toward a hearing. Simmons, addressing it on a later podcast, said he hadn't been aware of the proxy-betting rules and called the episode a "lesson learned."

No penalty has been determined, and the Commission's vote only sets up a future hearing rather than any finding against Simmons or FanDuel. For everyday bettors, the case is a reminder that the geolocation and identity checks built into every legal sportsbook sign-up — covered in our guide to how geolocation actually works — aren't just a technical formality. They're the line regulators use to decide whether a given wager is legal at all.
